maintopic: PATENT, TRADE MARK AND DESIGN, COPYRIGHT AND TIMBER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: Hon. A. K. MACLEAN (Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 150, respecting the Patent Act, the Trade Mark and Design Act, the Copyright Act and the Timber Marking Act.

maintopic: PATENT, TRADE MARK AND DESIGN, COPYRIGHT AND TIMBER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Explain, please.

maintopic: PATENT, TRADE MARK AND DESIGN, COPYRIGHT AND TIMBER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Until a year ago the Patents Branch was administered under statute by the Minister of Agriculture, but' last year the Patents Branch was removed from the Department of Agriculture, as the then Minister of Agriculture desired that the deputy minister should be concerned with no public duties other than those relating to agriculture. The Patents Branch was then, by Order in Council passed under the War Measures Act, placed under the administration of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The purpose of this Bill is to give power to the Governor in Council to place that branch under any department of the Government or under any minister. The Bill also provides for the creation of the office of Commissioner of Patents, who will be the chief administrative officer of the branch. These are the only two amendments.

maintopic: PATENT, TRADE MARK AND DESIGN, COPYRIGHT AND TIMBER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Is there any change in
the mode of obtaining patents or trademarks?

maintopic: PATENT, TRADE MARK AND DESIGN, COPYRIGHT AND TIMBER MARKING ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There are no substantive changes in the Patent Act. I did think earlier in the session that it was desirable to make further substantial amendments to this Act, but, chiefly for the reason that very important changes are likely to he made in connection With patents by all countries after peace is signed, I thought it better to postpone any important amendments to the Act until next session.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.

speechtext: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 151, respecting certain appointments in the Post Office Department.

subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: This Bill is introduced at the request of the Postmaster General (Hon. P. E. Blond-in) to meet the situation created by the withdrawal of a number of postal employees in Winnipeg, Calgary, and Saskatoon from the service during the month of May. Members of the House will recall that it became necessary, in order to maintain the postal service, to take on a number ol men in these post offices, and a number ol men were taken on, mostly returned soldiers. It was not possible, if the public service was to be carried on, that these men should be required to take the ordinary examinations; there was not time for it. The object of this Bill is to authorize the Civil Service Cbmmission to appoint to the public service in the Post Office Department those who were taken on temporarily at that time, provided that they are recommended by the Deputy Postmaster General and that the postmasters in these different cities certify that they are efficient in the performance of their duties.

subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext:
Is there not in the
present Civil Service Act a provision that that may be done legally in case ot emergency?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: No, the Civil Service Act as it stands does not cover the present situation. This is to appoint them permanently; under the Act as it stands, they might be appointed only temporarily. In order to secure the necessary men for these positions the postmasters in these cities felt that is was necessary to assure the men that their positions would be permanent; that they would not be dismissed in a few weeks' time.

subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: Does the Bill provide for similar emergencies in the future, and it not, why not?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: The Bill does not contain any provision dealing with the future. I understand that the amendment to the Civil Service Act, which is now before the House in the form of a Bill introduced by the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. A. K. Maclean), contains provisions which cover cases of a similar character arising in the future.

subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: This is an exception to the Civil Service Act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: Yes, to meet the exceptional conditions that developed in May last.

subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: Might I ask the minister if this is only to apply to men already appointed to the service? It is not intended for future appointments, is it, under similar circumstances?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext:
It applies to any one
who may have been taken on to fill vacancies in the service in these three post offices in the month of May last.

subtopic: RTI ,T. TO ENABLE PERMANENT APPOINTMENT OF P.O. EMPLOYEES IN CERTAIN WESTERN CITIES.
speechtext: Confirmation of appointments, I understand.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTH WEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT.
ROYAL NORTH WEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT.

speakeroldname: Hon. N. W. ROWELL (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTH WEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the amendment made by the Senate to section 8 of the Bill to amend the Royal North West Mounted Police Act, appears to have been made to some extent under a misapprehension. The object of the Senate was to introduce into the Bill an amendment of the same character as they introduced into the Militia Pensions Bill. It was not necessary, because the Bill already contained a provision dealing with the matter. I should, however, point out to the House that the Senate amendment goes somewhat further than the provision of the Bill itself, and I shall point out wherein it does so. The Bill itself prevents the widow or dependents of any member of the Force receiving a pension under the Mounted Police Act and also under any Canadian Pension Act. The amendment extends that provision and would prevent them from accepting a pension from the Government of Great Britain or of any other portion of the Empire-and also a pension under this Act.
I have conferred with the Comptroller,, and from the standpoint of administering the Police Force and in the public interest, we think that the amendment is not desirable, for the reason that we frequently get into the Force men who have served overseas, residents of the British Isles, who may be pensioners to a limited amount for services rendered in the British army, and.

if this amendment prevailed, their widows and dependents would be compelled to elect between that pension and the pension they would receive under this Bill. So far as the Police Force is concerned, we do not feel that any pension or gratuity which any member or his widow or dependents might receive from the Government of Great Britain should necessarily be taken into' account in dealing with the situation here. Therefore, I would move:
That the House do not concur in the Senate amendment, the matter having been already provided for in the latter part of section 8 of the Bill.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: ROYAL NORTH WEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT.
speechtext:
There being some question as to the precise form which a motion of this character ought to take, I would suggest, if it be agreeable to the hon. minister, that the order stand for the time being while we make sure of our procedure.
Motion stands.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.

speechtext:
On motion of Hon. Mr. Rowell (President of the Council) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Resolved, That it is expedient to provide in the proposed Act respecting' the Purchasing of Departmental and other Supplies and Materials for His Majesty, (Bill 46), now before the House, that the Chairman of the Purchasing Commission for Canada shall be paid an annual salary of seven thousand dollars, and each of the other commissioners shall be paid an annual salary of six thousand dollars, and that such salaries may be paid monthly out of any unappropriated moneys in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: When the Bill was before the House, we discussed the matter at some length, and certain clauses stood over for further consideration, it also being understood that in committee the principle of the Bill might be discussed if any hon. member desired to do so. I think that was on the suggestion of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). What I would suggest to the committee, if the committee would consent, is that this resolution go through in order that it may be referred to the committee for consideration with the Bill, and the whole matter may be discussed when the Bill comes back into committee. As a matter of form, it is necessary to get this resolution into committee so that it may be discussed with the Bill.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: I was unavoidably absent at the time, but after reading the debate, I remarked that the clause relating to the number of commissioners had been amended by substituting the words "not more than three'' for the word "three." By this resolution is it not intended that the number of commissioners to be decided by the clause in the Bill shall be entitled to the respective salaries mentioned in this resolution? My impression was that if we were asked to pass a resolution authorizing the expenditure of money, the amount had to be definite and the number of positions, for the emoluments of which the amounts were to be paid, had also under the rule to be definite. If We do not know how many commissioners are to be appointed, if that is left to the discretion of the Governor in Council, it is very hard to appropriate moneys for officials who might not be appointed at all.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that this resolution does not deal with the appropriation. There will have to be a vote in the Supplementary Estimates for that, and the number of commissioners must be determined before the Government introduces in the Supplementary Estimates the necessary appropriation. The effect of this resolution will simply be to provide a salary of $7,000 for the chairman and salaries of $6,000 for any other commissioners who may be appointed. It is necessary, as a matter of form before we can consider that clause of the Bill, to have a resolution of this kind. The number of commissioners will be determined before we bring down a Supplementary Estimate dealing with the matter, which can be discussed further, if my hon. friend so desires, when the Bill is in committee.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: All right.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
That safeguard which the President of the Council-mentions as regards the voting of the money does not seem to be necessary under this resolution, because it says:
And that such salaries may be paid monthly out of any unappropriated moneys: in the Consolidated1 Revenue Fund of Canada.
That would appear to me to give license for the payment of the salaries of these commissioners out of any money that is unappropriated. Therefore, if it is necessary that we should specifically know what amount of money is to be paid for this service, the amount ought to be named, because this resolution gives carte blanche to get it anywhere if it is available at all

and not earmarked for any other purpose. While I do not want to obstruct the work of the minister or the progress of the Bill on that ground, this is the first time in many years that a resolution for a money Bill was introduced at this stage. I have been . in this House for a long time now, and I never before saw a case where, if a resolution was at all regarded as necessary, such resolution was not introduced first and passed by Ithe House before the Bill was introduced. There may be some prq-vision for this, but there is nothing in the rules about it. Of course, there is what might be regarded a.s common law education in the books dealing with Parliamentary procedure, but the minister will find, if he consults those authorities, that he has not followed the practice. The clauses dealing with the money part should either be left blank altogether in the Bill or be printed in red ink so that that would be a blazing notice to everybody that this Bill was something apart from the ordinary procedure. Here we have a Bill printed in the ordinary way and the only blanks in it are blanks for the salaries. I understand they have had such cases in England, and the other procedure was followed, namely, the money provisions were left blank altogether or written in red ink to give notice to the House that there was something to follow. I cannot understand why the time-honoured practice was not followed in connection with this Bill just as in connection with any other Bill regarded as a money Bill which has been introduced into this House for many years past.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
I have repeatedly in this House referred to the ease with which high salaries in new appointments have passed through this House. It has come to be a hobby with me, and I have made many a fight for the man who is getting only $600 a year, with probably a wife and five or six children to support, and who finds it very difficult to get an increase. He is thrown over practically as a man undeserving of any consideration by the House, and he cannot fight his own way through the departs ments except on a set grading starting very low. I notice this resolution provides for an initial salary for the chairman of $7,000. Why should that not be $6,000? It shows $6,000 salary for each of the other commissioners. Why should that not be $5,000? We are burdened with debt in this country; the cost of living will probably soon come down, and yet we are establishing a principle of the highest grade of salaries after
the war is over as though the war were to continue for ever. I believe a man can be got as Chairman of this Commission for $6,000 as good as a man who is paid $7,000. Especially as we do not know who the man is, it is unwise to my mind to set a grade of salary which is going to be followed throughout the departments of this Federal Government.
It is an example that everybody else will be able to point to and say, " I want $7,000 for the .position I hold, because this commission has set a new standard." I think that is a pernicious example to set; it is not economical, and I think the House should be plainly told before this resolution passes who the man is that the Government propose to appoint, what experience he has had, and what is his general fitness fof this position. I am not making the argument that the salary is necessarily too high for' the position, but a general argument bearing upon the salary question. I can conceive that if this commission is to perform its functions to the best interests of the country, before we are through we may require a man who would not accept less than $25,000 a year; but that is not my point. My point is that we are appointing a man at $7,000 a year and we have absolutely no idea who he is. That is a radical advance to my mind, and will be an incentive to every other branch of the public service to reach the same starting point. I have said before in this House that the $600 man receives no consideration. When a Bill of this character was under consideration some time ago I made a direct apipeal to the President of the Privy Council, and he replied that the re-classification would take care of the $600 man. I have not had time to analyze the report, and I should like the minister to say before this resolution goes through whether the re-classification will better the salary of the $600 man.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
Dealing first with the remarks of my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition, of course I cannot speak from experience in this House as to what the procedure has been in the past. I can only say with reference to the form of this procedure that it is the form advised by the Parliamentary Counsel as being the proper procedure in a case where the salaries had not been fixed when the Bill was introduced. The amount of the salaries was left blank in the Bill showing that they had not been fixed, and the resolution was introduced subsequent to the introduction of the Bill, but before the Bill had been consid-

ered in the House and as soon as the salaries had been fixed. I know that it was a very common practice in the Legislature of Ontario, of which I was a member for many years, to leave the money clauses of a Bill blank until the resolution was introduced. When the resolution had been passed it was referred to a Committee of the Whole House for consideration with the money clauses of the Bill.
Coming now ;to the question raised by my hon. friend from North Perth, I do not now recollect just what the provisions of the reclassification are, but I do know that the position of the men my hon. friend refers to is substantially improved under the reclassification. If my hon. friend will turn up the report which has been laid on the table of the House by the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce he will see what is there proposed, and what is there proposed is not all that the men drawing the lower salaries will secure. There will also be a war bonus, which must be added to the amounts mentioned in the schedules, until the cost of living more nearly corresponds with what it was before the war than it does to-day.
Coming now to the question of the salaries of the Purchasing Commission, my hon. friend says, and very properly, that if we are to secure a man possessing the ability and experience which we should hope to secure for the chairmanship of this commission, we might have to pay a very substantial sum to secure him. I quite agree; I do not believe we could get a man of the ability and experience required for $7,000, if $7,000 was the only consideration, and he was dependent on that amount for his support; but I think we can make an appeal to public spirited citizens of this country, to* some of our business men who have been willing to give war service in the past and who would be willing to serve their country at this time for a reasonable amount, having regard to the fact that they are rendering public service as well as receiving compensation.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: Have the War Purchasing Commissioners received salaries in the past?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
No, they did not receive salaries, and I might say that none of the existing commission will serve in the future. One, unfortunately, has died, and the other two, for business reasons are unable to continue. My hon. friend asks why the salary of the Chairman has been fixed at $7,000. There is one reason; it may not be a very good one. Personally I thought

the amount should be higher, and I have no hesitation in saying so, tut $7,000 is the salary of a Cabinet Minister, and the view prevailed that we should not fix the salary of the Chairman of the Commission higher than that of a Cabinet Minister; so $7,000 was agreed upon.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: Cabinet Ministers' salaries are too low.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: I agree that they are too low, but that is the situation.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: Raise them.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: I have frankly told my hon. friend how the $7,000 was arrived at. There is this further fact, that $7,000 is the salary of the Chairman of the Civil Service Commission, and it was thought that these two commissions might be put on a parity. Any other commissioners appointed, whether it be one or two, would receive $1,000 less than the chairman, which is the salary the Civil Service Commissioners will receive,

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
I understood that there is a purchasing committee in each department; are these committees to be done away with? What I' should also like to know from the minister is this: About a year ago some men were appointed to re-classify the Civil Service, and it was understood their report would be presented to Parliament by the 1st of April of this year.' In view of the fact that the Government knew that that report was being prepared, why is it that in the meantime some men have received increases ranging from $100 to $2,000? Why were their salaries increased before the report was brought down? My opinion is that this country is being run altogether too much by commissions. There is one other commission which I think the Government would appoint if we gave in to them, and that is a commission to tell us how to vote. I want the money of this country saved and conserved. Our public debt is large, and there are many men throughout this country to-day who are sacrificing because they know we owe so much. Why is it that cabinet ministers do these things that can only cause dissatisfaction in the Civil Service? Any one who has looked over the report must realize that nothing could' do more to create dissatisfaction among civil servants. Some men are granted salary increases ranging from $100 to $2,000. In one particular case, a civil servant who was receiving $1,000 less than another man appears in the	report as entitled to $300 or
$400 more than this other man. The

head of one department is getting $5,000; and the head of another department $4,000; and the report of the Classification Committee says that the man getting $4,000 should get $4,800, and the man who is receiving $5,000 should be given $4,500, or $300 less than the other. Will this Government allow this sort of thing ? If we want satisfaction among the people and among the civil servants, we must do something to stop that kind of thing. If we allow this condition to continue, considerable dissatisfaction will be caused. This is a very drastic step we are taking in the appointing of so many commissions. We do not know how many men are going to be appointed. We were told a year ago that there were to be three, and now there are two more, and as I am informed this addition is absolutely unnecessary and will result in nothing but a debating" society. But in addition to these new men, there will be stenographers and clerks, and altogether the people are being called upon to pay thousands of dollars for many things that are entirely unnecessary. I think it is all right that we should try to pay every civil servant what he ought to get. The hon. minister told us they would give this man only $7,000, because Cabinet ministers w/re getting only $7,000, but the classification says that the deputy minister can get as high as $8,000. Why did the hon. minister not raise the chairman another thousand to put him on a level with the deputy? That would be only fair. I hope we shall have fewer commissions and that the people's representatives in this House will have some say in what is going on, and not have Bills, as happened last year and this year, forced through the House in the dying hours of the session, when we expect Parliament to prorogue. We do not know what legislation is coming down, and it is only fair to the members of the House that we should be given some idea of what is to be done in the dying hours of the session.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: Before this discussion goes further, I must remind hon. members that this is certainly not the proper time to discuss the classification of the Civil Service. It has very little to do with the resolution before the House, to which I would ask that remarks be confined.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was just answering the minister. He took the matter up and I think I had a right to reply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: I did not call the hon. member to order. I merely asked that other hon. members should not discuss the Civil Service Report.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: The hon. member has raised an important point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
The point is not
raised at the proper time.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
There is another point
that I would raise:	What will be done
with the present purchasing agents of the various departments when this new commission takes charge? Are these men to continue to draw large salaries as in the past, or will their services be dispensed with? We have purchasing agents in every department, some of them very efficient men who are conversant with conditions and prices of goods which they have been purchasing for years, and I would like some information as to what the intention is in this regard.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: I do not think my hon. friend was in the House on the second reading of this Bill, but if he would turn up the debate that took place on that occasion he would see that the matter was fully discussed. If my hon. friend does that and is not satisfied with the explanations and the statements then made, the whole matter can be reviewed when we get into Committee on the Bill.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
How many purchasing
agents are there already appointed for the several departments [DOT] of the Government, and will they still act as separate agents if this commission is appointed?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: That matter is all explained in the debate we had. There was a lengthy discussion of some hours and all these matters were dealt with. The total number of employees at present in {ill the departments of the Government dealing with the matter of purchasing is in the neighbourhood of 300. I am not sure of the exact number, they deal with purchasing, receiving, inspecting and passing upon supplies.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: The resolution provides that the Chairman shall receive $7,000 and the members of the commission $6,000. The number of commissioners is not determined, but there is a maximum number who may be appointed. This is an absolutely new expenditure over and above the present expenditure. These three men are being given powers already exercised by the ministers in the various departments, who are being paid salaries, small if you like.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
It is new and additional, but we are convinced, as the old commission which recommended this is convinced, that the net result will be a substantial saving in the actual cost

of administration, by a combination of all these branches into one. But the greatest saving will be in the actual purchasing of all supplies for the Government where they can be purchased in larger quantities at the same time for all departments requiring the same classes of supplies.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
I understand that, as I
read the discussion that took place on the previous occasion. But I contend that we are paying $19,000 for administration over and above the expenditure under the old system. Whether or not the Commission will be a matter of economy can be discussed in the Bill, although I see that opinions differed very much on the question. It has been claimed that there have been extravagance and mismanagement, but that can also be discussed in the Bill. I am merely pointing out that this is an additional burden of $19,000.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext: It is an additional expenditure which the Government believes will enable them to reduce the existing expenditure.

maintopic: PURCHASING OF DEPARTMENTAL AND OTHER SUPPLIES.
speechtext:
This is a proposition that ought to be opposed at every stage. I opposed the Bill as strenuously as I could when it was before the House and I intend to oppose it again, and I oppose the resolution. The minister will find that instead of reducing expenses of the various departments this will send them sky high above what they are to-day. I would imagine that deputy ministers and ministers, who are ordinary individuals; should' have pride in seeing their departments economically and properly managed in the matter of purchases. If the heads of departments have no responsibilities at all ' except to pass orders over to an outside commission who will buy goods and pay the prices, there will be a keen rivalry between the departments to obtain things of the greatest excellence which they would do without ii they had to shoulder direct responsibility themselves for the purchase of them. We are creating an institution to buy for all departments, and it is absolutely impossible for the Commission to know the requirements of the departments, or whether an order sent to them is reasonable or not. I cannot conceive of any difficulty in a deputy minister sitting for ten minutes in consultation with a man who is selling goods. He knows what he wants and the man is willing to sell to him, and he surely can get goods as cheaply as they are going into the market anywhere else. I am clearly of [Mr. R.owell.J
the opinion that this is absolutely a mistake. I am sick and tired of hearing of people serving their country for nothing. We have heads of big concerns serving the country gratis so far as salary goes, but they are drawing grist to their mills in other ways ten thousand times greater than their salaries.
I hope we have heard the last of this extraordinary patriotism that is abroad in this country. When this thing is inquired into we find that the man who has served without compensation has simply served as advance agent of a circus, or something else, to find out the best way to put up his posters. In like manner, these high patriots find their way into the departments and government positions and simply utilize those positions for the advancement of their own business, or to put money in the way of their friends. Whether they are getting a rake-off from it afterwards I am not going to say, but that is what is going on. It is better for this Government and this country to hire a man who has no such high ideas of patriotism, pay him and let the business of the country be done in a business way. We had never heard any complaint about the departments not doing their business properly until this War Purchasing Commission arose and found that they were in a position to do big things and to do them in a different way from what they had been done before. I look for no good from it at all. I would say, as has been said already by hon. gentlemen supporting the Government, that this is no time for extravagance or plunging into new experiments involving hundreds of thousands of dollars. The minister has been honest enough to tell us that he must increase the staff of this new department- and that he must start with something like 300 or 400 men and women. He proposes to take whatever number of men are engaged in that commission now and pitchfork them into this new service over the heads of the Civil Service Commission, and, in that way, violate the law. Although there is no doubt that this resolution will pass, my good friend from Durham -I think it is-says that the next thing will be the appointment of a commission to tell us how to vote. I think there are sufficient commissions abroad now to tell hon. gentlemen supporting the Government how to vote on this resolution. All we can do from this side of the House is to protest against it. It involves extravagance and the unnecessary expenditure of money at a time when every dollar should count in the judgment of the Government, and particularly

*when we are in the financial position that we are in to-day.
I submit to the Government that if any private concern were in the financial condition that the Government is in, it would be regarded as hopelessly insolvent. I say that seriously. What would we think of a merchant, a manufacturer, or a man at the head of any industrial concern in this country, whose finances were in the condition of the finances of the Government, plunging into unnecessary extravagance of this Kind? 1 submit that there is not one financial law to be applied to the Government and another financial law to be applied to every going concern in this country. The Government should cut their coat according to their cloth and when money is low and hard'to get, and the cost of living high, it should get along with the least possible expense. For this, and many other reasons, which have not yet developed, but which will develop under this Bill, I submit that it should not be passed at all. As for myself, I am determined to do everything I can against the piling up of any expenditure for this year, or possibly next year, that we can get along without.

Mr. Chairman, 1 cannot sit quietly in my seat and allow such aspersions as we have listened to, to be cast by the hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie) upon the men who have given their services free of charge for the last five years. I know man after man who has left his business, who has been under great financial loss, who has come here to Ottawa, and slaved as he never worked for himself, while our boys were at the front, actuated only by patriotic motives. When the leader of the Opposition arises here and imputes to every one of these gentlemen sordid motives and alleges
that they were endeavouring to bring grist to their own mill he does something that he ought to be ashamed of. If there is anything that we shall look back to when this war is over with credit to ourselves it will be the fact that we had men in Canada, not five, or ten, or twenty, but scores who were willing to sacrifice their own private interests in the public cause while this war was on. I can point, as every one knows, to man after man who, when he goes back from Ottawa, having served at his own expense for the term of years that he has given to this service, will go back and live a quiet life, for the rest of his days, simply because there is nothing left in him. Let me just say one word in respect to the chairman of this War Purchasing Commission, a man from my own province whom I have known all my life as a man of the highest integrity and patriotism; he left a big business, left his family, came here and worked twelve months in the year for five years in order to save this country thousands of dollars as the head of the War Purchasing Commission. For any one ito tell this House or this country that that man had some sordid motive other than 'the desire to render patriotic service is to make a statement that is umvorthy of the House and unworthy the leader of a party.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.

speechtext: Hon. HUGH GUTHRIE (Solicitor General) moved the second reading of Bill No. 138, to amend and consolidate the Acts relating to British Nationality, Naturalization and Aliens.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
At the risk, Mr. Speaker, of making an unpopular suggestion, I submit that we should not be compelled to discuss this Bill ait the present time. The Bill, which is a very important one, was introduced on Wesdnesday of this week, only three days ago. Its most important sections are based on the Imperial Act of 1918, and 1 went to the library and tried to get that Act in order that I might study the Bill and give it proper consideration. I was told, however, that there was only one copy of the Imperial Act of 1918, and that it was in the possession of the Solicitor General (Hon. Mr. Guthrie). Of course, being a plain private member, I could not compete with my hon. friend in the securing of that book, and I do not think it is fair to the House or to the country that this Bill should be forced through three days after its introduction and before we have had time or opportunity of studying it and considering its various provisions.
iMr. GUTHRIE: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
Technically, under the
rules, the Solicitor General exhausted his right to speak when he submitted the motion. I take it, however, that the House will concur in permitting him to make his explanation.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: 'Certainly.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
I recognize that upon
a casual reading of the Bill, it would appear to be somewhat involved and to require a good deal of consideration. However, I may explain that the Bill is merely a consolidation of the two Acts now in force in Canada in respect to naturalization, to which has been applied the Imperial Act of 1918, the precise language of the various sections of the Imperial Act being employed as far as possible. I have prepared a copy

of the Bill showing precisely, by indicating them in red ink, what are the clauses of the Imperial Act, and showing by marginal notes the verbal changes in each section. It will be remembered that a few days after the outbreak of the war-I think on the 7th of August, 1914-the Imperial Government passed an important Naturalization Act. This Parliament had passed an Act on the 24th of June, 1914, without knowledge that the Imperial Parliament contemplated any action in the matter. After the Imperial Act had been passed, this Parliament passed a further Act, on the 22nd of August, 1914, at the short summer session, to bring into force in Canada certain sections which had been adopted by the Imperial Parliament on the 7th of August preceding. On the 8th of August, 1918, the Imperial Parliament passed a further Act by way of amendment of the Imperial Act of 1914, and the two Acts now in force in Great Britain are cited as the British Nationality and Status of Aliens Acts, 1914 and 1918. It is provided in the Imperial legislation that any self-governing Dominion of the British Errfpire may adopt Part 2 of the Imperial Act, and that if it does so, a naturalization certificate thereafter granted in that dominion shall have force and effect throughout the whole of the British Empire; but until the Parliaments of the various self-governing dominions expressly adopt the provisions of part 2 oi the Imperial Act, certificates of naturalization granted in the self-governing dominions shall have force and effect only in the British dominions in which they were granted. The matter was discussed at the last Imperial Conference, and it was generally agreed that a uniform naturalization law would be in the interests of every part of the Empire; but it was recognized that each dominion had a perfect right to regulate the matter for itself, so far as its own jurisdiction went. However, from a discussion which took place in the British House of Commons, I learned that practically all the self-governing dominions had expressed their intention to adopt part 2 of the Imperial Act. I do hot really know how many have actually done so, but I think all save Canada and Australia. However, I am not certain in that respect. The main change effected in the Imperial law was in regard to the revocation of certificates heretofore granted, and in regard to the status of married women. We know that in Canada, prior to 1914, under the provisions of our law certificates of naturalization were 242
granted after residence of three years. In 1914 we changed that law and made the period of residence five years; that is, in conformity with the requirement of the Imperial Act. But the Bill which is now before the House has included in it only the provisions of our own law passed in June, 1914, and in the following month of August, and in addition thereto the provisions of Part 2 of the Imperial Act, without any change whatever in .the language except so far as is absolutely necessary to make it applicable to Canada. For instance, the tribunal in England which deals with the question of revocation of certificates, is not identical with the tribunal which will deal with those certificates here. Mere matters of form of that kind have had to be changed, but in other respects the language of the sections included in the present Bill is identical with the language in the British Bill.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: What tribunal deals with the revocation of certificates in England? We have not had a chance to see the Imperial Act.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
In Great Britain under the Act of 1918 the inquiry in regard to applications for the revocation of certificates is held by a committee constituted for the purpose by the Secretary of State. This is the language of the section:
An inquiry under this section shall be held by a committee constituted for the purpose by the Secretary of State, presided over by a person (appointed by the Secretary of State with the approval of the Lord Chancellor) who holds or has held high judicial office, and shall be conducted in such manner as the Secretary of State may direct:
The language of that section would of necessity have to be changed in a Canadian statute.
My suggestion would be, if the Bill is given its second reading, that discussion in Committee go forward and that any reasonable time should be allowed members to make comparisons and further investigate the Bill, But until we can discuss it clause by clause, I do not think more can be gained by amplifying the general explanation which I have sought to give the committee. I know it would help very much in considering the Bill if this copy were used*, and I would like to hand it to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition so that he can see the manner in which the Bill has been consolidated.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Are there many copies ol the Bill that my hon. friend is proposing to turn over to the leader of the Opposition? I see it is a printed document.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I made this single copy myself. Any one can do the same who will take the time. It is only to indicate the clauses in the Imperial Act that are not law in this country now, but which will become law if this Bill passes. This also indicates the necessary change. The other sections are all sections passed by this Parliament in 1914 and prior years.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I understand from my hon. friend that this is a consolidation of the Canadian Acts, with the addition thereto of part of the Imperial Act to make a Canadian a British subject in any part of the Empire. The Act of 1914 was passed under war conditions, and we then departed from the very basis of the other Acts. Heretofore our tribunals have been granting citizenship; if a man wanted to be naturalized he had to go before the courts. To-day we have taken away that jurisdiction from the judiciary and placed it in the hands of a political body-the Government or the Secretary of State.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I think if my hon. friend will read the section he will find he is mistaken. A man desiring to become naturalized still has to make application to. the courts. The old Act was passed before the war, on the 34th of June, 1914. We have left the war-,time procedure behind us.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I did not notice the change, I think applications for naturalization should not be left to the decision of any political body, neither should .the revocation of certificates of citizenship. Under the Imperial Act which my hon. friend has just read the Secretary of State may appoint a committee under the Lord Chancellor or some man with judicial experience-some one who would be above any political feeling.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Our Bill provides for investigation by the judges of the superior courts in the various provinces.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Only if the Secretary of State thinks fit.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: No. There are four distinct cases; in three of them the Secretary of State is bound to cause an inquiry to be made; in the other case-and it is the case only of a man who has been out of the British Dominions for seven years and has not kept up any connection therewith-the Secretary of State may cancel the naturalization papers. But these are matters that can be discussed in committee, and I do not think we can very intelligently deal with them on the second reading.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I was about to call the attention of the House to the rule that on the second reading only the principle of the measure can be discussed. We are departing from that rule in this case and are discussing the effect of certain clauses.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
I want to say on the second reading that I am against the principle of this Bill as indicated here. I am of opinion that these powers should not be left in the hands of the Government or of any politically organized body; the judiciary is the best tribunal to decide whether certificate of citizenship should be granted or refused. I also wish to register my most emphatic protest against the provisions in regard to revocation. If a man becomes a citizen of a country he is supposed to abide by the laws of that country, and if he commits such offences that revocation of his papers should be necessary, I think we ought to be able to make laws to remove such a man from society, instead of throwing him out of the country without any citizenship at all. We ought to think twice before taking such drastic steps and telling a man: " You foreswore allegiance to your native country; you have failed to observe the laws of this country to which you swore allegiance; therefore you are an outlaw." It is far better, if that man is so dangerous that he ought not to live in Canada or any other part of the British Empire, that you should jail him. Let us make laws to punish a man according to the offence he commits. We have power to do it, and we ought to exercise that power. To revoke a man's citizenship and place him in the position that he has no citizenship, that he is, in fact, an outcast, nationally speaking, is so drastic that in my opinion he would be better off in jail or dead. Any offence which merited revocation of citizenship might merit life imprisonment or the gallows.
He is better dead, and if any offence is such as to merit the revocation of a man's certificate of citizenship, it might merit a jail sentence for life, or even the gallows. We can pass laws here which will cover every such case. I wish to register my protest as regards the principle of this Bill on this ground, and possibly on other grounds, because I have not yet had time to study the Bill which I regard as a most important one. This Bill, which is going to determine the citizenship of a man, was brought up on the 18th of June, and we are called upon to-day to pass upon it and discuss the various conditions. We have not had any opportunity to look into the Imperial Act or to see the conditions upon

which that Act was framed and what the conditions are in this Bill. I do not know the opinions of the other members, and I am not going to call for a division, but I desire to object to the principle of the Bill as brought before the House.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I could not quite follow my hon. friend's argument in his earlier remarks, but I understood him to make a protest against the Act as it seemed to depart from the old practice by placing the naturalization of persons into the hands of political parties.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I said a political body, not party.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: My hon. friend surely cannot mean that, because the fact is at the present day the Act under which we have been granting hundreds and hundreds of certificates-I am signing about 1,200 a month-is the new Act of 1914.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: That does not change my views.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
That is an Act which this House passed. In the previous Act what happened was this: Commissioners on naturalization were appointed, and they could simply take a man's affidavit that he had lived in the country for three years, he having been in that district for such and such a time. He took the oath of allegiance; this was handed into the court; a list was prepared; at the end of the court the list, comprising perhaps 100 or 200 names, was read out by the clerk without any examination of the applicants being had; the matter went through almost pro forma, and, in fact, numbers of naturalization certificates of this kind were known to be handed out in blank, no care being exercised. In 1914, that Act was changed by this Parliament, and, as a matter of fact, it has been in operation under much more satisfactory conditions since, because the old Act and the new Act were allowed to run concurrently for three years, from 1914 to the end of 1917, as it was thought that those men who were naturalized for Canadian citizenship for three years should be given an opportunity of taking up their homesteads under the old Act. But the new Act, under which we have been acting since 1914, and which was the only Act since January 1, 1918, instead of providing the old method, has provided a method under which naturalization is infinitely better safeguarded in the interest of this country than it ever was before, because the Act says this: A man shall pass in his application
242i
for citizenship, for naturalization, to the court; a three months' notice shall be given; that notice is sent to the Secretary of State, and the judge has then to hear the case for naturalization. The man has to have been residing for five years in Canada; he has to have an adequate knowledge of either French or English and to be a person oi good character, and the judge has to satisfy himself on all those points. It is, I think, obvious to every hon. member that it is a most important matter, especially in view of what has taken place in this world during the war, that the naturalization and citizenship of every person should be of an absolutely irreproachable character. It is a thing we have to safeguard. No political party has had an opportunity of advancing its own interest under the Naturalization Act which has been in force for the last few years. The judge has to decide according to the provisions laid down in the Act. That is, therefore, not a new feature; it is simply embodied in this Bill which, as the Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) said, is simply to consolidate the Acts and also to embody the provisions which he has mentioned regarding revocation. No hon. member would argue that there should not be any power vested in the Government of a country to revoke naturalization where naturalization has certainly been improperly bestowed. That is a principle we could not accept; the details of that will be taken up in the clauses of the Bill.
Brigadier-General GRIESBACH (Edmonton West): Mr. Speaker, there is an aspect of naturalization to which I should like to direct the attention of the House, although I am not sure whether it might come up properly at this time or later. I refer to the question of the status of aliens who apply for naturalization, who come from a country in which there is legislation that prevents the alien from becoming a British subject even if he is naturalized here. I refer particularly at the moment to my understanding of the Delbriiek law which obtains in Germany. By the provisions of that law, as I understand it, a man may be naturalized in Canada or elsewhere, but he still remains a citizen or subject of Germany with all his rights in Germany and with his responsibilities in Germany, and particularly the responsibility for military service. The situation was that, when the war broke out, citizens of Germany, impelled either by motives of patriotism which are to be commended, or because of the operation of this law, sought to Teturn to Germany to bear arms and,

in many oases, succeeded in getting back to Germany and bore arms, a matter as to which some of us here can testify. I remember, in 1915, in trenches opposite a position which I held, Germans from the trenches shouted out inquiries as to conditions and persons in Edmonton, and we had reason to believe they were men from that city. Pressure is exercised under those laws in those foreign countries in this manner. A man is liable for military service notwithstanding the fact that he is naturalized in Canada, and if he does not return when his call is made, they confiscate all his property; they imprison him should he ever return to his own country again; they provide that he shall never be able to inherit any property in his own country; they deal even with his relatives and friends, and they bring pressure to bear upon him in every conceivable way. Indeed, it has, as a matter of fact, been found that the law is very effective. I am strongly of opinion that this country cannot afford and ought not under any circumstances to give naturalization to any man who comes from a country where a law exists that makes it impossible for him to become a citizen of this country,'and this Bill should especially provide that no certificate shall be issued to any person who comes from any such country, the law of which makes it impossible for him to become a citizen in fact, in law and in every other respect.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the second time.
On motion of Hon. Mr. Guthrie (Solicitor General) that the House go into Committee on the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: The reason I ask is because the Imperial Conference passed a resolution that another conference composed of the representatives of the United Kingdom and the Dominions should be called in order to agree upon a uniform law of naturalization. Is this Bill the result of such a conference?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: No. The Bill was passed by the Imperial Parliament after it had been approved by the representatives of the Dominions, but there were two or three points that were considered of importance which w'ere not covered by the Imperial Act, and the conference to which my hon. friend has referred was called for the purpose of considering those particular points. I do not just recall them at the moment, but I think I indicated them when we were discussing the report of the Imperial Conference.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Did the representatives of the Dominions agree on these outstanding points?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: No conclusions have yet been reached on those points, and they are not embodied either in this Bill or in the Imperial Act. They will be covered by subsequent legislation.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
Take the case of an alien residing in territory annexed by the British Government. It is altogether likely thait the British Government will annex or control for some time East Africa, for instance.

What would be the status of a German resident in that territory?
iMr. GUTHRIE: This Bill would not affect him one way or the other. This Bill only deals with those who have become British subjects by reason of annexation. There might be reasons why the people of that territory would not become British subjects, but any one who had become a British subject would have the privilege of continuing one under this Act. When the Imperial Act was introduced by the Secretary for the Home Department on the 12th of July last, Sir George Gave said:
This Bill was approved in principle at the Imperial Conference in the spring of 1917. Since that time a draft Bill has been circulated throughout the Empire and the draft has been approved by all the self-governing Dominions and India, with the exception of Australia, which has not yet approved the draft, but has indicated no dissent to it. The main purpose of the Bill is to introduce wider powers of revoking certificates of naturalization.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
Paragraph (c) says:
Any person born on a British ship whether in foreign territorial waters or not.
Now if the policy of the Government is to establish a Canadian merchant marine, would it not be well to insert the words " or Canadian " after the word " British " unless "ia British ship " includes the ships of all the Dominions?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
I think the clause as
drafted would cover every ship sailing under the British flag. The restriction here is in the case of a birth occurring on a British ship in <a South American port, for instance. The object of this restriction is that a person born on board a foreign ship shall not be deemed to be a British subject simply by reason of the fact that the shifp was in British territorial waters at the time of his birth.
iMr. BUREAU:	Suppose a British subject is naturalized in the United States, and a child is born to him while there. The next day he moves to Canada and becomes a British subject here by naturalization. Would the child take the. citizenship of his father when he reached a certain age?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: The status of children and married women is dealt with in subsequent sections of the Bill, beginning at section 11.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
But the provisions have to be read as a whole, and that shows the necessity of going through the Bill very carefully. I understood from the President of the Privy Council that further legislation
is to be brought down next year covering certain points that were to be dealt with at an Imperial Conference,

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
What I said in answer-to my hon. friend from Kamouraska was-that a committee had been appointed representing all portions of the Empire to' consider certain questions which were not covered by the existing legislation, and that no final conclusions had yet been reached by that committee. When final conclusions are reached by that committee, they will have to be embodied in new legislation.
(Section agreed to.
On section 2-Certificate of naturalization.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Subsections 5 and 6 are entirely new and are taken verbatim from the Imperial Act of 1918. Subsection 5 is taken from 5 George V, and subsection 6 from the Imperial Act of August, 1918.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
I move:
That Section 2< subsection 1 be amended by inserting the following proviso after subclause C:
Provided that under no circumstances whatever shall a certificate of naturalization be granted to any person, a citizen or subject of a foreign state in which there exists a law, rule or regulation which qualifies limits or restricts the citizenship by this Act conferred or in any way exacts or requires from such foreign applicant military allegiance or service to such state on the event of threatened or actual war.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
That would hardly be appropriate in the present section. If my hon. friend will give me the proposed amendment I will consider it. It would be more properly inserted about the end Of ' part 1. I move that consideration of it be allowed to stand in the meantime. I will see that it is submitted at the proper time.
Motion stands.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Subsection (b) provides that any one- who is of good character may be granted a certificate of naturalization if he has an adequate knowledge of either the English or French languages. It does not say anything about other languages, and in the great war we had other Allies than the French. For instance the Italians were our allies. Are they to be excluded?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
This is only a matter of making persons British citizens. Before the war the opinion of this Parliament was that they should be familiar with the English or the French language, and in Great Britain, they have confined it to familiarity with the English language. I think that there should be some familiarity with either

'the English or the French language provided for.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
The languages of the
country.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
Yes.
On section 3-Effect of certificate of naturalization :

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: How does this affect the Oriental?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I am not aware of any law that provides for the naturalization of .Orientals in this country.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: The Oriental at the present time has no vote. Under this section he would be allowed to vote.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
I am not prepared at
the moment to answer that question. I shall have to inquire into it and answer it at a later stage. I was under the impression that they had no right to be naturalized or to become British subjects.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
There are two or three
thousand Japanese in British Columbia who have taken out naturalization papers but they have no vote.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I think I can answer the question now. I understand Orientals have a right to be naturalized in Canada, but under certain local laws of the province they are not enfranchised, notwithstanding their right to be naturalized if they comply with all the requirements.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
The naturalization does
not give them the right to vote.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: No. It does not change the laws in force for the last thirty years.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Give them the provincial franchise and it would be all right.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Take the case of women- an Indian woman is a British subject. What would be her status? Would she be deprived of the right to vote by special legislation in this Bill? If she can exercise all the rights of a British subject she should have the right to vote, because under federal enactment all women who are British subjects and who have reached the age of twenty-one have the right to vote.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: When we come to the Franchise Act that will be a fair matter to deal with, but not under .this Bill.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
If it is thought wise in the provinces to limit the franchise to certain nationalities there might be a contest with

the provinces. If a certain class of Orientals are given all the rights, powers and privileges of British citizenship, we would be passing a law that would perhaps be inconsistent with provincial franchise laws.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: The Franchise Act of a province can apply only to its own provincial franchise, which is beyond the jurisdiction of this Parliament.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I want to avoid the possibility of the Dominion franchise being different from the provincial franchise, and there might be a contest. By passing this law what will be the situation in regard to Orientals?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: All these questions relating to franchise can much better be discussed on the Franchise Bill. They are not relevant under this section.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
Suppose there is no
Franchise Bill?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: When it comes.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Political rights are mentioned in this section and the franchise is therefore relevant.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
We confer all political
rights on a person on naturalization. If any province, having jurisdiction, desires to limit the franchise in regard to persons who are not naturalized, it has the full right to do so under our constitution.
If in the province of Ontario they passed a law to exclude an Oriental from voting, or from exercising the provincial franchise, they would have a perfect right to do so. But they have no right to pass any enactment that limits or alters the Dominion franchise. We grant a certificate of naturalization to an alien and if a, province did not want that alien to vote it would say so, but in so far as this Dominion is concerned, as soon as we grant the certificate we clothe the person to whom the certificate is granted with all the rights of a British subject.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: If an Oriental in the past has had a right to vote in federal elections that right has never been exercised and British Columbia would not desire that it should be exercised.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: The provincial lists were used in the federal election according to the old Election Act. That is why Orientals do not vote in federal elections.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: That is the reason.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
If we use the provincial lists for federal elections they have the

right to vote unless you deprive them of that right.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
The right to say who
should exercise the franchise in federal elections was delegated by the Federal Parliament to the province and that right will still be exercised by the province unless the delegation is cancelled and the Federal Parliament takes into its own hands the duty of legislating for that purpose. But, when a certificate of naturalization is given to a Chinaman, Japanese, or Hindu, that man gets the full rights of citizenship the same as any other man.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: There has always been a provision in the law about conditional naturalization. I am speaking of the case of a man who receives full naturalization.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I think the limit of five years should be raised because I do not believe you can take a Chinaman or a Jap and make a good citizen out of him in five years.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: You must adopt that period of time if you are going to make the provisions uniform throughout the Empire. Great Britain will not recognize our right unless we conform to their general scheme. Otherwise, our naturalization will be purely for Canada.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Why not get them to raise their limit?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: They were requested to but they have definitely made the term five years and it will have to be adhered to.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: I think that is a dangerous standard to set up.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
Five years is two years
longer than it used to be; it is raised from three years to five.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
The time is
altogether too short.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
Is there not some safeguard in the discretion of the court? Even if a man had been here for five years, if the Secretary of State, or the court, think he is noit a desirable party to receive a certificate, I think they can refuse it.
M. FIELDING:	There has been a distinction between the status of a British subject in Canada and a British subject in England. Is not the object of this to put them both upon a common plane?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: There will be no such distinction in the future?

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: No, it "will be the same throughout the Empire. I move that the Committee rise and report progress. In the interval perhaps we will have an opportunity of studying the matter more carefully.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext: Will that be before Tuesday?	.

maintopic: BRITISH NATIONALITY, NATURALIZATION AND ALIENS CONSOLIDATION AC'T.
speechtext:
No, not till after Tuesday?
Progress reported.

maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ROYAL NORTHWEST MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Referring to the Mounted Police Bill which was up this morning- I beg to move:
That this House doth disagree with the Senate amendment for the following reasons:
The amendment is inconsistent with the provisions of the proviso to clause 8 of the Bill and unduly extends the restriction contained in the said proviso.
And that a message be sent to the Senate to acquaint their honours therewith.

Motion agreed to.
