maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: On motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean, the House went into Committee on Bill No. 53 (from the Senate) to amend the Proprietary or Patent Medicine Act, as amended by Special Committee, Mr. Stevens in the Chair.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: What was the result of the sending of this Bill to the Special Committee?

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The report of the Special Committee, with suggested amendments, was submitted to the House some time ago, and the amendments have been printed and circulated among members of the House. The amendments recommended by the committee are substantially in line with th; views expressed by a majority of the House when it was up for second reading. The committee have recommended that the sale of opiates containing opium or derivatives of opium be absolutely prohibited.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Before he went away the member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) made reference to the fact that certain hon. gentlemen, including, I think, the member for Muskoka (Mr. P. McGibbon), had taken a

particular interest in this Bill. I understand that the subject matter which the hon. gentleman had in mind was with reference to drugs containing opium or other narcotics. Are the proposed amendments incorporated in the Bill?

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
We propose to incorporate the amendments in the Bill. I am accepting absolutely the recommendations contained in the report of the Special Committee, which, I understand, was unanimous.	'
On Section 7-Prohibited medicines.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not understand exactly how we are proceeding. Are you reading all the amendments?

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I might explain that practically the whole Bill is one section amending various sections of the Act.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think section 7 is subject to some discussion.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
In subsection (g) "It
the article to be represented as a cure for any specific disease," we are going further than the law of any other country. The United States regulation on this subject is usually considered the most stringent, and it provides that the preparation may not be designated as a cure unless, as a matter of fact, it can be depended upon to produce the results claimed for it. I venture to say if you pass this clause you will have a whole lot of trouble. If you want to wipe out patent medicines that are no good, I might suggest to my hon. friend (the Acting Minister of Trade and Commerce) to not go any further than the United States and the British law.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The section, as
amended, will prevent the advertising of any drug as a cure. We are going just as far as the United States, but I think we are putting ourselves in a better position, although the legislation is practically the same.
The United States legislation is to the effect that patent medicines must not contain any false, misleading or exaggerated claims on the wrapper or label. It is very difficult to prove that. It is doubtful if any medicine is a cure for anything. Medical men who are members of the committee assured the committee' that there was practically no such thing as a medicinal cure for any specific disease, except, perhaps, three or four. The effect of the United States legislation is to prohibit any

advertisements of a patent medicine as a cure, and it is quite proper that we prohibit the advertisement of any medicine as a cure. This does not prevent manufacturers from selling their product.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think this would prevent a manufacturer of anything like antitoxin from selling his product.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Antitoxin is not a patent medicine it is one of the things that might be denominated as a specific cure. A patent medicine is a medicinal preparation which is patented, and the formula is not disclosed to the public. If the formula is disclosed to the public, the preparation is not a patent medicine.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The reason that the medical men object to the word " cure " is practically what the minister states except that he goes further. Most of them state- and I think correctly-that there are only a few medicines in the world, such as antitoxin, which cure disease, and they are not patent medicines, they are medicines which are usually used. In the past manufacturers have quite often put up patent medicines representing them as cures. For instance, a manufacturer may put up a patent medicine representing it as a cure for consumption when, as a matter of fact, there is no such thing as a cure for consumption, and inestimable damage has been done to the people of this country by advertising such patent medicines as cures for consumption. The elimination of the word " cure 1 will do no harm to the patent medicine manufacturer, and it will give protection to the public whom we are only safeguarding in taking this stand.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not think you can enforce this to the limit, because journals and periodicals printed outside of this country contain advertisements of medicines, the announcements claiming that the medicines are cures. How are you going to regulate in a case of that kind? If you discriminate against advertisements appearing in Canadian journals guaranteeing these medicines as cures1, the owners of these proprietary medicines will have to go outside for their' advertising mediums, and they can have their announcements published in English journals and those of other countries.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
This Bill will
prevent the importation of any .medicine which is represented as a specific cure for any particular .ailment. It cannot prohibit the advertisement in foreign journals of any

medicine which is asserted to he a cure for anything. Clause 7 begins by stating:
No proprietary or patent medicine shall he manufactured, imported, exposed or offered for sale or sold in Canada if-
As in this particular instance,
-it is represented as a cure.
So the public are protected in that way.. They can have the pleasure of reading in foreign journals advertisements about these medicines promising a cure, but that is all.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Will that prevent an individual from sending outside for them?

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Yes.
Mr. PETER MicGIBBON (Muskoka): 1 think I said the last time this Bill was up that the only object of a Bill of this kind is to protect the public, and I submit with all due respect to the minister that this clause does not give them any protection at all. It is rather around this clause that all the curse of patent medicines hinges. It is quite true that formerly we had a number of medicines advertised as cures for certain diseases, but that time has long since passed away, and now a manufacturer simply sets down' symptoms which are peculiar to a certain disease and advertises his medicine as a cure for those symptoms, and that is far more effective than advertising it as a cure for any particular disease. This clause opens the door to all kinds of fraud, and innocent people will be imposed upon by the hundreds and thousands, and this clause ought to be eliminated.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
If we eliminate this clause, there is no protection whatever for the public. As the subsection- stood in the original Bill, it read:
If the article Ibe represented as a cure for any specific disease.
The word " specific " is stricken out in the amendments recommended by the Committee, so that the result of the amendment is that no patent medicine can be manufactured, imported, exposed or offered for sale in Canada if it contains the representation that it is a cure for anything, so that this is a positive enactment against representing anything as a cure for any ailment. If we strike this clause out altogether, then there is no protection for the public, and manufacturers can import and expose for sale any medicine represented as a cure. I thought my hon. friend did not quite understand the situation.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I
quite understand the situation, but probably I did not make my point clear. This allows manufacturers to get around the purport of the Bill by simply changing the wording of their advertisements. The objections taken a few' minutes ago are quite in order, namely that we ought to follow the lines laid dowui in Great Britain and the United States, or else we should put in a clause specifically prohibiting manufacturers from advertising a medicine, not as a cure, but as a relief for any specific set of symptoms, because that is the line all these advertisements are taking now. A manufacturer does not advertise his medicine as a cure for consumption, but the advertisement w'ill describe the symptoms of tuberculosis and then describe the medicine as a cure for them. There is no protection for the public at all.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The intention of the committee was to eliminate the word " cure " altogether. It is possible, as the hon. member says, the word might be used as a cure for symptoms. You cannot eliminate advertisements of medicines claiming that they will give some relief, because they may give some relief to certain symptoms of certain diseases.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: If you follow the law as it is in the United States and. in England, you would have more effect.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
We have also this clause containing a prohibition against any representations of a false, misleading or exaggerated character being used on the label or wrapper. That is really the American provision. The Americans do not make an enactment against the use of the word " cure They state simply that no false, misleading or exaggerated claim shall be printed on the wrapper or label, and under that clause, they presume to prohibit the use of the word " cure ". We have specifically enacted against the use of the word, so that we are in a much clearer and stronger position than the United States, and besides that, we have their clause for what it is worth. If you attempt to prosecute a vendor of patent medicines on the ground that the wrapper or label contains misleading or exaggerated claims, it is, in my judgment, a very difficult thing to prove. I think iwe have in this Bill everything of importance in the American Act. We are also specifically providing against the use of the word "cure." Unless I had an opportunity of giving further consideration to the suggestion of my hon. friend, I would hardly care to accept it. We are en-
382a

acting pretty sweeping legislation, and I thing it will meet the case.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I submit again that I am not interested in the manufacturers of patent medicines, but in protecting the public from deception. If I were a patent medicine manufacturer I would not want a different law from this.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am unable to agree with my hon. friend. We are specifically providing against the use of the word "cure" for any disease, and I think under that provision we could prosecute a man who advertised a cure for the symptom of any disease.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I know something about the drug business, but I am thankful to say I have absolutely no connection with it ' now. I certainly think the minister will have a lot of trouble if he leaves the Bill as it is now, and I would suggest that he add after the word " disease," in paragraph (g), the words " unless it can be depended upon to produce the results claimed for it."

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I fail to see how a direct enactment against the use of the word "cure" is not better than an enactment against the use of that word with the qualification that my hon. friend has suggested. If we adopted his suggestion, it would be very difficult to secure a conviction. I am assuming that my hon. friend wishes to prevent the sale of patent medicines representing to cure certain diseases.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Take the case of jaundice, for instance; that is not a disease but a symptom.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I am told there is no cure for jaundice.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not like discussing medical questions on the floor of the House, as it smacks of talking shop, but as my hon. friend has mentioned jaundice, I agree that it is not a disease but a symptom. There is no distinct cure for jaundice, because it arises from many different causes, and anybody who advertised that a medicine would cure jaundice would come under the clause against exaggerated advertising, because there is no one thing that will cure all types of jaundice.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I trust that the minister will accept my suggestion to add the words I have pro,posed to paragraph (g). That will be as far as the British and the United States law goes, and the Swedish law, too, I believe. It is the only way you can deal with patent medicines.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I would direct the attention of the committee to subsection 2 of section 7. One of the matters that was urged in connection with this Bill was the necessity for curtailing the use of medicines containing opium for children. Subsection 2 says:
No proprietary or patent medicine intended for administration to infants under one year old shall contain any opium or any derivative of opium, or any derivative of coal-tar.
I think the weakness of that subsection lies in the wmrd " intended." Intended by whom? A manufacturer may put up a soothing syrup exactly along the line of the old-time soothing syrup and disclaim any intention of its being administered to a child under one year of age. The mother, knowing that it is really the same soothing syrup, or that it will have the effect of quietening her child, which she desires, buys it, and administers it to her child just the same as she did formerly. She is not responsible' in any way under the law. It seems to me this subsection is absolutely useless for the purpose for which it was intended, and I w'ould suggest that it be amended in order to meet the views of many people, and especially of the social workers of the province of Quebec.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Section 6 says:
All proprietary or patent medicines containing opium, or any derivative of coal-tar, and intended for administration to children over one year of age shall he labelled with the words " Dangerous for infants under one year old."

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Possibly that covers the situation.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is any penalty provided for an infraction of the provisions of this Bill?

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: There is a general penalty clause in the Act.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-new section 7A.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: It is provided that five members shall be appointed on the Advisory Board, and I think that pharmaceutists actively engaged in the drug business should be represented.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
That is a fair suggestion.
Mr. FOURiNIER: It should be made plain.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think it is good legislation to specify any classes of persons who shall constitute the membership of a board to be appointed under the law. The department must be trusted to

select the proper 'personnel. I quite agree *with the suggestion that the class mentioned by the hon. member should he represented.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The druggists, who number about 5,000 or 6,000 in this country, are respectable citizens and are entitled to consideration. It is no more trouble to include druggists actively engaged in pharmacy than it is to insert the Dominion Analyst.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The statute does not designate any particular class for the board. We simply state that the chairman of the board shall be the Dominion Analyst, and he is the official of the department administering this and similar Acts. When the department constitute the board they will have in mind, of course the particular interests of the pharmaceutical profession in Canada. Personally, if I were asked to give an opinion, I would say that they are entitled to representation on a board of five, but if you say that one particular class shall be represented, you must stipulate in the Bill what other four classes shall have representation. The statute framed in that way would be unsound and too restrictive.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I think that men
actively engaged in the drug business should be represented. After all, we copy the United States in many ways, and there you will find that pharmacists are represented on boards of similar character, being represented even on the Board of Health.

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I do not mind saying that they will be represented.

speechtext: What Act is repealed?

maintopic: PROPRIETARY OR PATENT MEDICINE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
There was an Act known as the Doherty Act which contained a clause that had reference to patent medicines, and that should not have been in that Act. The amending Bill at page 3 in the second last paragraph contains an amendment by inserting immediately after section 16 a provision to the effect that any penalty incurred under the provisions of this Act shall be deemed an addition to and not in substitution for any penalty incurred under the law of any province. That is the section which we are repealing and which is in chapter 19 of the statutes of 1916. We are taking it out of one Act and putting it into this, because it has relation to patent medicines.
Bill as amended reported.

What are the subsidies under this item, and what trips will be made, and so forth? I should like some information in this respect.

This is a combination of services that were performed last year under separate services and separate votes. It means no increase whatever. It is a re-arrangement of old services. It does not mean an additional vote of money. The contractors have not been able so far to perform the Newfoundland end of the service. They were to call at Prince Edward Island, Pictou, Mulgrave or Hawkesbury proceed through the lakes and on to Newfoundland. The company have been unable to obtain a steamer suitable for the service but we are hopeful that they will be able to do so any day now. At the time the contract was entered into last year it was thought that the steamer leaving Quebec and calling a't ports of the south shore of the St. Lawrence would proceed:- en route to Newfoundland but the company have been unable to do that. Later, they asked to be allowed to take a portion of this subsidy and apply it to a direct service between Quebec and Newfoundland via Prince Edward Island and Cape Breton ports. While, up to the present time they have been unable to get a steamer to go on the service, we are hopeful that they may get one any day now.
Will the minister name the ports that they call at in Nova Scotia?
I find I was in error in saying that there were several ports in Cape Breton that the bo^t would call at. Apparently there is only Sydney.
What is the name of the boat that used to perform that service?
It has not been performed for several years. It is a revival of an old service that was performed by some of the Dominion Coal Company boats.

The Black Diamond
line?

The Black Diamond line. Very strong representations have been

made by the people of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland and Montreal for the establishment of this service but unfortunately it has been impossible up to date to get a steamer to perform the service. There is no service but I am asking for the vote so that it may be available at the time that a boat is available.

If this service is to
be established, I want to make a strong appeal to the minister to have the boat call on the western coasit of Cape Breton. I think that the boat might call at Chet-icamp. It is right on the route to Sydney. The only question is whether there is enough water and, due to the fact that there are no boats, we cannot discuss that feature of it. The boat that usually comes down there calls at that port. There is 21 feet of water. There is considerable amount of freight to be carried and if the boat calls at this port, it would give connection between that part of the country and the port of Sydney.
Mr. A. K. MAOLEA'N: If my hon. friend will be good enough to write a letter to the department covering that matter it will be inquired into.
I will do so.

I am not in a
position to give him any more definite answer. If Cheticamp harbour has not a sufficient depth of water to accommodate the steamer that would be a sufficient answer. I think that the Newfoundland subsidized services from Nova Scoia require rearrangement. There are too many different subsidies voted.
At what pout in Newfoundland will the boat call?
iSt. John's.

Does the minister say
that St. John's is the objective?

In this service.
There is a subsidized service to Newfoundland, I think from Halifax. They go through the Bras d'Or lakes and then on to some port on the west coast of Newfoundland.

I do not know that it is good business to send boats around to St. John's from Quebec unless it can be shown there is really business to be done. There is a line of boats running between North Sydney and Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, connecting with the line of railway across the island of Newfoundland unless it was found that the rail-4 p.m. way and the Reid line are unable to cope with the traffic

and that there is business to be done it would hardly be desirable to add another subsidy.

There is a very
real demand for a steamship service between 'Canadian ports and Newfoundland at the present time. The Reid-Newfound-land company are unable to handle the-traffic arriving at North Sydney for delivery to their railway system. Great quantities of goods are now in Canada which should have been in Newfoundland months ago. Owing to the inability of the Reid company to handle the traffic, the Government had before it yesterday a representative of the Newfoundland Government who was here to ask that we loan them temporarily a boat to run between Sydney, or North Sydney and St, John's so as to relieve the congestion on the Reid-Newfoundland line. It will also be helpful to the Intercolonial railway. I think the Minister of Railways, or the Canadian National Railway Board, was enabled to meet to some degree the request of the Government of Newfoundland. There is a great congestion at the present time.

The route between
Canada and Newfoundland is established as far as North Sydney is concerned because the trade converges by rail at North Sydney. If it is necessary to add a further boat to carry the goods -from the terminus of the Intercolonial railway at Sydney to Newfoundland I think it is good business but I do not think it is good business to start a boat from somewhere on the river St. Lawrence calling at intermediate ports and then going to North Sydney to take on goods. The railway is quite capable of handling the traffic going out through North Sydney and which can then be carried by boat across to Newfoundland. *

There is a considerable quantity of goods being purchased for Newfoundland in Quebec and Ontario. There is apparently a very substantial amount of business in Prince Edward Island which goes to Newfoundland. The steamer en route can call at Charlottetown. Later, I suppose, when the Reid-Newfoundland Steamship Company are in a position to purchase more steamers, they may be able to relieve the congestion. Our trade with Newfoundland is developing and Canadian merchants are anxious to maintain and improve their position in that regard. Unfortunately, we have not yet been able to get this additional steamer.

The trouble is that at Port aux Basques the facilities are not adequate. Moreover, the steamship service which is now proposed to be subsidized will carry quite a different class of goods from that which has been handled by the ships of the Reid Company. Cattle, for instance, could not very well be transported by the boat *engaged in this service between North Sydney and Port aux Basques.
*Steam service from ISydney to Bras d'Or Lake ports, and ports on the east and west coasts of 'Cape Breton, $14,000.

This is a new service which will be performed by a company now operating from Sydney. It will be a weekly service. The boat will leave Sydney, proceed through the lakes, and to points in Northern Inverness, and then run to Sydney via the south and west coasts of Cape Breton island.
What are the ports of *call?	.

Sydney, North Sydney, Baddeck, Grand Narrows, Marble Mountain, Castle Bay, East Bay, Big Pond, Irish Cove, Johnston's Harbour, St. Peter's, Poulamond, Grandique, Port Hawkesbury, Port Hastings, Port Hood, Mabou, Mar-garee, Grand Etang, Cheticamp, L'Ardoise, Ariehat, Gabarus, Louisburg, Main-a-dieu, Port Morien, North Sydney and Sydney.

If this was a service
all-around the island of Cape Breton, commencing and ending at Sydney, I would look upon it as a splendid service. But the ports which the minister has mentioned are already served by subsidized boats. For instance, that part of the Bras d'Or Lakes south of the Grand Narrows bridge is served by the Richmond.
The Richmond has been taken off and is replaced by this new steamer, which will carry out the service formerly performed by the Richmond. The new boat is larger and faster than the Richmond.

A service such as the Richmond was giving in that part of the Bras d'Or Lakes should not be changed at the whim or caprice of any steamboat owner. The people have been getting a service; it is the money of the people that is being paid out in the granting of these subsidies, and merchants and others interested should be consulted. They were getting two trips a week from the Richmond, which is a very good little boat; now they are to get a weekly service simply because
the owners of this boat think that they can make money in that way. When traffic or trade routes are established by a service subsidized by the Government, that service should not be thrown aside for something less serviceable without giving the people concerned an opportunity of expressing their views in the matter.

I have been
under the impression that this new service would be more satisfactory to the people of the ports concerned than was the service rendered by the Richmond. It is a very much larger boat.
She worked very well.

She probably had to call at these ports in order to carry freight, and consequently had to make two trips a week. However, if it transpires that this service does not meet the local requirements, it will have to be reconsidered.

We have a Government creamery at the town of Baddeck. The great body of people on the Bras d'Or lakes south of the Grand Narows used to send their cream by the Richmond to the Grand Narrows and then it was transferred to the Blue Hill, and there must have been three or four trips a week. If there is only one trip that service is absolutely abolished.
Has my hon. friend any objections to the changed service?

If it is less efficient than the old, I certainly have. Those people are not in my county, but the creamery is, and it is a Government creamery. If this new boat is giving less efficient service to the people than the Richmond was giving, I certainly object to the change.
Would the minister be good enough to tell the Committee the total amount of money that is paid out in steamship subsidies?

In round figures the total amount to be paid this year is $2,400,000. Of course, that includes all sums paid for services on the Atlantic and the Pacific, which form the greater part of the total I have mentioned. After all, the moneys paid out for subsidies to local services in the Eastern part of Canada do not amount to very much. I cannot give my hon. friend exact figures.

I am not particular about what is paid out in the East; I merely want the total. Have the Government control, and do they exercise control,

over the tariff arrangements made by these boats with the people who trade with them? If so, what is the nature of the control ?
We have a very decided control over freight rates. In the first place, the freight schedules must be approved by the Government.
What department?

The Department of Trade and Commerce. For instance, we subsidize a service between the British West Indies and the ports of Halifax and St. John. We fix their rates. The rate on flour per barrel is ninety cents, and it has remained so during the war, constituting a decided advantage to Canadian millers. It was a cheap rate, too. It has the effect of keeping the freight rate on flour from points in Canada to the British West Indies via New York at ninety cents, and had we not control of the rate charged by this subsidized service, the freight rate would be very much greater to Canadian exporters of flour.

Do I understand that the rates are fixed by the Department of 'Trade and Commerce, and that the department are in a position to know what rates should be charged along the Pacific coast and the Atlantic coast without having some official set aside for that purpose?

All subsidized services must have their rates approved by the department. They submit their freight schedules to the department for approval, and the department advise themselves in the best way possible as to the fairness of those schedules. We have an inspector of the local services, in regard to which it would be most difficult to ascertain whether the freight rates are fair or not. So far as the Atlantic and Pacific freight rates are concerned, it is not a difficult matter for the department to be advised as to what are fair rates, because they are in touch with the commercial rates and can secure the advice of men competent to advise them.

I am puzzled to know the extent to which these rates are examined into from time to time. While I know the Department of Trade and Commerce are very efficient in so many ways, I qan hardly believe that they can possibly be in touch with the conditions existing at the different ports of entry that these boats are connected with, and I would be surprised to know that the department were able to control the shipping rates in the

sense that the Railway (Commission control railway rates.
Our control is absolute to this extent, that unless a contractor will enter into an agreement with ,the Government as to the rates to be charged by him, he cannot get the subsidy.
Does he file a schedule of his rates with the department?
Yes.

I am struck with the disparity in these items, Mr. (Chairman. I know the services very well. There is a most important service under item 184, from Sydney to Whycocomagh performed by the steamer Marion. While I do not want to disparage the service rendered under item 185, I submit it is not one whit as important to that part of Canada as the service performed between Sydney and Whycocomagh. I cannot reconcile those votes. Then there is the service performed by .the same people who expect to run this new boat between Sydney and the Bay ISt. Lawrence, along a rocky coast; they are to get only $6,000, against $14,000 for the service under item 185.	i !	j
The supplemental will contain an additional $1,000 for the service.	'	\

My hon. friend knows the island of Cape Breton and the service performed between Sydney and Whycocomagh, serving a large number of people along the Bras d'Or Lakes. The owners of the boat get only $3,000 for that service, while the other service is subsidized to the extent of $14,000.

Might I ask the minister to kindly jog the memory of the Hend-ric Company, Halifax, I think, about which I wrote the minister a few days ago? This service is performed by the Strathlorn, which carries the goods past ports such as Margaree down to Chetieamp and Grand Etang, and if the weather is not sufficiently fine, carries those goods back to Halifax, and they are dumped down upon the wharf there. Such conduct is unjustifiable, and I do not see why they should be permitted to do such a thing. More than that, this year they have departed from their obligation as regards carrying out their contract to Inverness and have gone into another service, to Guysborough, which is entirely different, carrying goods to way ports, and return-'ing to Halifax without going to Inverness ports at all back (when it suits themselves.
If this be true, I would ask the minister to eee ito it that this is stopped or the boat he discontinued entirely. We are dependent upon that service.

The company will be asked for an explanation.
Trade and Commerce-trade commissioners and commercial agents, including expenses in connection with negotiations of treaties or in extension of commercial relations : miscellaneous advertising and printing, or other expenditures connected with Canadian trade, ? 180,000.
What is the increase for?

This increase is asked for just to have the supply necessary if any extraordinary expenditures are undertaken during the year in the way of development of Canadian trade abroad and by way of establishing additional trade commissioners. It is quite improbable that the additional amount will be used this year. Since the termination of the war, however, the department is frequently in receipt of requests to send trade commissioners to many new places with a view of ascertaining if it is possible to develop trade in those places. One would expect that these requests would be made at this time when all nations are contesting very keenly for commercial supremacy in all parts of the world. I thought it would be well that we should have, perhaps, a small amount in addition to that of last year for this purpose. At the present time, I cannot say that it will be used; it does not look as if it would be this year.

The statement was made by the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) the other day that some $6,000,000 was expended by the Government in financing the sale of meat to Italy. Can the minister tell us what prices are being paid to producers of this, meat and from whom it has been purchased?

I think it was my hon. friend who asked the minister about this matter or, perhaps, it was some other hon. member, and upon his request I laid upon the table of the House this forenoon a copy of the Order in Council to which I would refer my hon. friend. I think it will give him the information he desires.
Does this Order in Council give the names of the parties from whom the meat was purchased?
No, I do not think it would do that.
Can the minister furnish us with the names and the prices the meat was sold at?
I cannot promise to do it to-day, but I would be in a position to do it on Monday.
Is the meat taken from cold storage warehouses?

This was meat that was purchased in anticipation of sale to the Allied powers for army purposes, and, in fact, I think the Allied powers were morally obligated to take this meat. When the armistice came, the demand was reduced very materially, and the meat was on the hands of the contractors, who endeavoured to sell it to the Canadian public, but I believe they were unable to do so almost at any price. The British Government, my recollection is, undertook to make a disposition of it so far as they could, and they entered into some arrangement with the Government of Italy whereby they would take this quantity of meat that was in cold storage in Canada and which was in danger of being destroyed altogether or becoming useless. It was for that purpose the Canadian Government gave credit to Italy.

I understood the minister to say that the British Government was handling this business and that the meat had to be sold and that Canada undertook to finance the transaction. Is the Canadian Government by taking this step relieving the Imperial Government of a responsibility?

This is a matter of business with which I have nothing to do, and I am speaking without accurate knowledge of the facts. I will send for a copy of the Order in. Council, and I will endeavour by Monday to get the further information for my hon. friend.

I must reiterate what I said to the minister some time ago about the sale of goods of this character or the sending of such goods out of the country. The law of supply and demand means the supply in a country itself and the demand in that country for that supply, or the demand that a foreign country might make upon that supply with its own means or money. The Canadian consumer was entitled to the competition, that would arise in this country in connection with the sale of supplies of food that were in this country and the Government is not dealing fairly with the consumer when it is furnishing money to a foreign country in order to buy

those goods and take them out of Canada, because that has certainly a direct effect on keeping prices higher than they would be if the matter was left to trade and 'traffic in this country itself. I cannot see any justification why the Canadian consumers are compelled by this Government to a foreign country, when that money is to be used for the purpose of keeping-prices at the high top-notch figures at which they are now. If we have a reduction at all by competition, it is 'by the supply 'becoming large and people toeing obliged to bid or do the best they can to get the current prices for their goods.
What method would the hon. member adopt to establish the proper balance between the producer and the consumer?

The law which exists and which is as old as the hills, the law which regulates itself as to supply and demand. If there is a large supply of beef in this country, and the merchant or [DOT] the owner of it cannot keep at his high prices in ordeT to get rid of it, he must sell at a lower price. But this Government steps in and says to that man: You need not sell at any lower price; we will keep you at war prices, and we will give money to foreigners so as to enable them to come into this country and buy that extra supply and take it out of the country and enable you to keep at your high prices. The law of supply and demand, as I understand it, is put out of operation in that way by artificial means, and I say that the Government of this country is not justified in doing that.

There are just
two views on the question which my hon. friend has raised. One is that no aid in the form of credits be given to -our export trade, and that it be allowed to operate as in pre-war days. The other view is that you assist the purchasing country to pay for our goods by lending them the money. My hon. friend says that we should allow the law of supply and demand to govern all trade and commerce. Every nation desires that, but there is no such thing in some countries to-day as the operation of the law of supply and demand. The question of wheat, for instance, which we are likely to discuss some day next week, presents a great many difficulties. We shall have a wheat crop this year of probably 300,000,000 bushels, and an exportable surplus of from 200,000,-

000 to 225,000,000 bushels'. Everybody knows that it is important that this Canadian wheat gets out o>f the country. Wheat is no better than any other product, except that dt is more useful as a food than some others, and the wheat producer has no right to expect better treatment than the farmer who is producing other products, but it is very desirable from the standpoint of exchange that the wheat should get out of the country, because it is one of our exportable products. If we export
200.000.	000 bushels of wheat, that means
8400.000.	000 coming into this country with which to pay for our imports from the United States, and therefore it is desirable that we should have a movement in our grain trade this year. But the Western farmer cannot export his wheat unless he gets paid for it in some way or other. Suppose that Great Britain says next September or October "We will not guarantee the price of wheat, and we have no way of buying your wheat unless you advance us tire money. We will buy of Argentina or of Australia, who are willing to give us a credit." If that event should occur the situation would he serious, unless we loaned Great Britain the money.
Money will never pay for the imports of a country. Great Britain's gold supply would be exhausted in a week is she had to pay for her imports in money. So while natural trade is desirable, and is better for producer and consumer, and the sooner all nations get back to it the better, still conditions prevail which prevent it and for which nobody is responsible. I quite agree with the views of my hon. frienl, but it may very well' happen that we may yet have to give credits to help our export trade. Where would Canada be to-day if we were not exporting what we are under the credits that were given last year. There would be a congestion in this country of our exportable goods, and production would immediately diminish, because there would be no encouragement to produce. However, that matter has been discussed several times in Parliament, both sides of the case have been presented clearly and ably, and the question is likely to come up again next week on the amendments to the Grain Act. The Government are not anxious to establish further credits to any other country. It may well be that we have reached the point where it would not be wise, and might even be impossible, for us to grant further credits. I can assure my hon. friend that

no one is more anxious to cease the granting of credits than the Government, because many difficulties are involved in securing the credits and taking care of their distribution.

The minister has not dealt with the main question at all, that this manipulation of finance maintains high prices. Does he expect to go on doing this or is he going to stop? If it is true that the granting of credits is the cause of the inflation of prices, every time a credit is granted increases the price to the home consumer. When is i't going to come to an end?

I think the end will come when we reach the time hoped for by the leader of the Opposition when natural trade conditions will prevail, when the nations of the world will be importing and exporting as they did before the war, when we shall again have international competition. When Canadian products are sold, the price is agreed upon by the purchasing country. If Canada furnishes credits for the purchase of Canadian products by other countries, we do not fix the price. There is such a demand, particularly for certain food products and some manufactured articles, that prices are extremely high to-day. Take the case of wheat. The fixed and guaranteed price in the United States for this year is $2.26; ours last year was $2.24. That is a very high price for wheat, but I doubt very much whether the world will ever see again the price levels of days gone by when wheat was selling below a dollar a bushel. Although $2.24 seems a high price, the view prevails that it is not an excessive price. When the United States fixed the price at $2.26 last year, they submitted the whole matter to a committee of eight very expert men, and it was their judgment that that was not an unfair price for the producer. I have discussed this matter with a great many Canadian wheat producers, and I am bound to say that I doubt very much whether it is an excessive price, particularly if there is a small or average crop. The cost to the farmer of producing wheat is exceedingly high at the present time, or at least very much in excess of the cost which prevailed prior to the war. I suppose that if credits were granted freely by governments to all countries desiring to purchase their goods it would have the effect of driving up prices, but no country is anxious to give credits to-day. The United States Government is not giving any, although they realize that somebody in the United States must make
advances to European countries or they would not toe able to sell. I cannot see how any European country can purchase anything of any kind to any extent unless somebody advances them the money.
We can all buy if you give us the money.
But these credits have to be repaid.

The minister is
speaking as if he were solicitous about the farmer, but i't is not the farmer that is going to be benefited by this transaction which we are discussing; it is the owners of the cold storage plants, who have hoarded up this meat to fetch a high price. The people of Canada needed this meat, tout the cold storage men would not sell it to them. They held it until, as the minister says, it was in danger of being destroyed, and then the Government steps in and furnishes money .to export it to Italy, financing the bills for Italy. I have no doubt Italy is just as able to do its own financing as Canada. Why does the Government do this for the cold storage people? It is not in the interests of the farmers, for not one dollar of this money will go into the pockets of the farmers; it will go to the profiteers. That is what makes it so difficult for the people of Canada to accept the situation. It is not only in regard to meat and wheat, but in regard to other things as well. I was speaking to a merchant tailor this morning and he told me about the difficulty he had in securing cloth to keep his business going. He said that if you went to one of the jobbers' shops there were half a dozen persons looking for the same web of cloth, and one man would offer $5 a yard and another $6. They would bid against one another because they had to have it. The mills are busy making cloth for Rumania, and the Government is borrowing money from the people of Canada to finance the business. The millers do not care anything about Canadian trade. They are doing very well by selling their goods in foreign countries. This has to stop, and the sooner the better.

I quite agree that it must stop, and the sooner the better. I am sure that it is the desire of all countries to get back to normal trading. But unfortunately there has been a war for four years or more and all trade and commerce has been disrupted and has been conducted for some time along artificial lines. I did not know when I was speak-



ing that my hon. friend had in mind this credit to Italy for the purchase of wheat. I was speaking generally of the policy of granting credits. I am [DOT] not very well acquainted wiith the facts concerning the sale of meat to Italy.
Who were morally obligated?

The British Government acting on behalf of the Allied governments. The producers in Canada were urged to get supplies together and have them ready for export, and the goods would have been required had the war continued. I understand that this meat that was sold to Italy was of such a quality that no purchaser could be found in Canada for it. It was known as "thin" beef and the owners offered it to the Canadian public at, I believe, very fair rates. I remember conversing one day with an hon. gentleman on the other side of the House who was engaged in this business in Quebec or Montreal, and he informed me that in that particular city

I think it was Quebec -you could not induce any one to purchase this beef because it was frozen or chilled. I shall endeavour to get the information my hon. friend requires about this sale of beef to Italy. I must repeat that I am not w'ell acquainted with the facts.

Are these bonds in the case of Italy taken at the same rate as in
the case of Rumania-5 per cent?
At 5J per cent.

I do not desire to delay the Committee, but it would be a mistake to allow to pass unchallenged the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cahill) and others. The hon. member's opinion that the trade policy of the Government at this time is simply pandering to the profiteer is absolutely unfounded. He evidently overlooks the fact that the market in Europe today is bare of goods of all classes, including foodstuffs, which must be supplied and will be supplied. Where will the supplies come from? Chiefly from the American continent, that is, from Canada and the United States. We can, if we choose, take advantage of this extraordinary position, by arranging Government credit-where private credit has been eliminated by the war-through no fault of the manufacturer or trader-in Rumania, Belgium and France, where the factories have been blown up and storehouses have been under German control for years. These business concerns have no organization or credit, -and the Rumanian, Belgian, or French Government, as the case may be, establishes national credit which this Government takes advantage of, and to the result of which I invite the attention of the hon. gentleman, because it is a matter of vital importance to Canada. Taking advantage of this dearth of goods in Europe, and being in the fortunate position of being able to supply those goods by the medium of Government credits replacing the shattered private credits, we are putting Canadian goods on the European market where they never were before. In other words, we are building up foreign trade. I have heard hon. gentlemen on the floor of this House chide the Government for not sending out more trade commissioners, and time and again attention has been drawn to Great

Britain, the United States, Japan and other enterprising counties that were spending hundreds of thousands of dollars in sending trade commissioners the world over to develop foreign trade, Now, here we have a perfectly natural opportunity to inject our trade into the European market. I come now to the point suggested by my hon. friend from Peterborough. The argument is advanced that we should not send goods to Europe at the present time under any arrangement of Government credits. It is contended that because there is a scarcity in Canada we should keep these goods here for the local market and prevent export. Let the hon. gentleman consider this point:
Supposing we shut off these Rumanian, French and Belgian credits, what would be the result? The American buyers would come over here, buy these goods, ship them to American ports, send them into Europe as American goods, and we would be in the same position as we are in to-day, except that we would not have secured an entry into the foreign market. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) smiles. I speak in all seriousness when 1 say that that is exactly what would occur.
That would be fine; we would get our money back then.

We would get the money back then? Then the hon. gentleman hinges his whole argument upon the point whether the French, Belgian or Rumanian Government will redeem their pledges. The hon. gentleman suggests that, because of the low value of the bond, this Government is selling goods worth 100 at 72. He knows perfectly well that that is-I was going to say a false argument-but I will say an inaccurate argument. These bonds may only be worth 60 or 70 or 80 but the value of the goods fixes the amount that is paid for them in bonds. If the goods are worth 100 in gold, and the bonds are worth only 72 in gold, they will have to make up the difference in bonds.
There is another point. We were told by the hon. member for Guysborough a moment ago that this Government was encouraging the cold storage companies to hoard up meats for the purpose of shipping goods overseas. I have absolutely no sympathy with the so-called packing institutions. I have no brief for them; in fact, if I could drag anything out of them to show that they had been doing wrong I would be almost pleased to do so. But still we ought, as a Parliament, and as the leading element in this country, to send forth to the public the facts. As near as I can

judge from the facts produced, the situation was simply this: There was a surplus of frozen beef last winter brought about by this condition, namely, that at the signing of the armistice current contracts-not prospective but existing contracts-were cancelled leaving, as it were in transit between the farmer and the ultimate market, large quantities of beef. My hon. friend suggests that the beef was spoiling, but experts of the Government have told us that this beef cannot spoil as long as it is-frozen and that it will keep in good condition for a long time. As to the hoarding of other stuff in cold storage plants, no evidence has yet been brought forward, so far as I have been able to learn, eithei before the Cost of Living Commissioner or before the special committee of this House, to show that there has been a hoarding of other foodstuffs in cold storage warehouses. If that is so, we ought to know it. Let mer just again emphasize this point at issue, which is all important in connection with getting into the European market, that if we fail to take advantage of the opportunity now, we will simply give the same privilege to the American traders and 5 p.m. will not be one whit better off in Canada as far as the shortage of food is concerned. It is infinitely better for us to sell our goods at their market value in order to establish a market for future trade, even at the cosit of a slightly enhanced value here at the present time. If there is anything that should be done by this Government at all it is the fixing of the spread ait home. That possibly is a matter that may be brought to the consideration of this House a little later on, but under no circumstances should anything be done to interfere with the establishment of a Canadian foreign trade.

The hon. member has
given the besJt argument in the world why we should discontinue these credits. He says that the American people would buy the goods. If they did so we would be paid for them. We would get our money at the rate of 103 cents on the dollar instead of 72 cents on the dollar. The condition, according to the argument of the hon. member, is that Europe is bare of goods. I tell him that the pantries of this country are bare of goods and it is our duty to see that the people have provisions at a reasonable

If the bonds are selling
at 72 we are not getting them at 72 but we are getting them at 100. Therefore we are losing the difference.

I suppose that we may expect that our dollar in New York will be iworth 100 cents but it is not so to-day; it is only worth 97. Thait condition of affairs prevails at all times and there is always fluctuation in the value of credit.

The very reason that Great Britain cannot buy to an unlimited degree in Canada is that the British pound is worth a,bout $4.60 and it is liable to go to $4 any day. If the rate of exchange was $4.86J Great Britain would not ask for credit for the goods she buys from us. The fact that Rumanian bonds are quoted at 72 does not prove that they will not be retired at par when they mature.

It is a mighty poor business man who pays 100 for bonds that are only worth 72. It is mighty bad business to send goods to some foreign country and take their bonds at 100 when they are only quoted at 72. There is no argument for that. The people must suffer as they are suffering. While you are telling the people that the dealers are not able 'to sell their meat in this country and that they are sending it to Italy, it is significant that the price has been increasing and is higher now than when the armistice was signed. If these dealers offered these meats to the
I Mr. Cahill.]
Canadian people they would find a ready market for them here, but perhaps the price would go down. Instead of doing that they have held them, shipped them to a foreign country and they have sold the goods on the strength of 'Canada's credit. When you take these credits which have been granted to Great Britain, that is a different proposition. The Canadian people probably owe Great Britain a billion dollars to-day, .taking into consideration the obligations of cities, corporations and municipalities. That is a matter of adjustment between Great Britain and Canada. But there is no adjustment between Italy or Rumania and Canada. When we sell goods to these countries we should take their money for what it is worth in the market. There is no question in my mind but that we are doing mighty bad business when we charge our people 100 cents on the dollar and sell to a foreign country the same goods at 72 cents.

The most serious question before the country to-day is the high cost of living and if we bonus certain industries at the expense of the general consumer the high cost of living for the consumer will not go down but will go up and there will be greater unrest than there is now. The hon. member (Mr. Stevens), at the close of his remarks, said that there is a great temptation to make use of, or to .take advantage of, the foreign market at the enhanced price. That is to say, the subsidized exporter is to have the benefit of this credit at the expense of the general consumer. But the general consumer will not stand for it. It is all very well to have a brilliant prospect, but it may be a rainbow dream; and that is what this is. If the money we were making by taking advantage of the foreign market and of foreign possibilities enured to the general benefit of the Canadian consumer, then the argument would be justifiable, but when ft is not so, you are, to use plain language, robbing the general consumer in order that the exporter may profit. The people of Canada are endeavouring to find out what the difliculty is, and when they find that it is because our butter, eggs, meat, and so on, .are being rushed to a foreign market which is subsidized by our own people, and that they are being tortured accordingly, I am very much mistaken if they do not rise up and call a halt, saying: The limit is the suffering which we have to endure and the extra high prices which we are asked to pay but which we refuse to pay. If we are going to play fast-and-loose with the affairs

of the country in this way and take advantage of a temptation which is only going to carry its own sting with it, any attempt to solve the difficulty will be hopeless.
There is a prevailing heresy amongst some members of this House that if you sell goods in a given market you can always buy other goods from that market; that people must have goods bought from them if they expect to buy goods from you, or you hope to sell to them. That takes no account whatever of the element of profit, all of which is comprised in the single phrase " rate of exchange." Everybody knows that when the rate of exchange is against a country, as it is against Canada and in favour of the United States at the present time, this country pays from $13,000,000, to $15,000,000 in hard cash for the privilege of having the balance of trade against it-and that is the very thing that has come up in this argument now. To my mind, it shows a complete absence of a grasp of the difficulties of the situation.

I read in the newspapers, or was told, that the grain elevators in the Northwest and at Port Arthur and Fort William were practically commandeered by Americans last year, that they filled those elevators with their grain to the exclusion of Canadian grain, and that that is causing stagnation of trade among our own wheat producers. Mr. MA.NION: The hon. gentleman is wrong in thinking that the elevators at the head of the Lakes were so used. said to have been the most presentable and spectacular of any that was shown there. We had fifty stalls where Canadian products were exhibited, and, as a matter of fact, by virtue of this fair, several millions of dollars' worth of goods were sold in France, tentatively.
For money?

What does the minister understand by "tentative" sale?

A tentative sale means this, that somebody in France is willing to buy goods of a Canadian manufacturer exhibiting at Lyons within a given time if the former could make arrangements to pay for the goods. The prospective buyer might be very well off, 'but on account of exchange conditions as between France and the rest of the world he might have no means of paying. A man might be worth many millions of dollars in France and still be unable to pay for a small importation of goods from Canada.

There are dozens of such "tentative" bargains every day. Every boy that passes the store down here has the inclination to buy, but he is short of the money as a rule. The credit should surely be inducement enough, without spending more money to get this trade for which we are getting in return no money and no goods.

The Canadian
people are very largely inexperienced in foreign trade. Grant to Canadian Engineering Standards Association for the promotion of uniformity of standards in metallic and other products, $10,000.
Is this a new item?

The Canadian Engineering Standards Association (incorporated 1919) is a branch of the British Engineering Standards Committee founded sixteen years ago and closely associated with the British Board of Trade. The British Engineering Standards Committee was brought into existence for the purpose of introducing uniformity (Standardization) wherever possible in taps, dies, chasers and screw threads, all types of rolled steel sections, such as beams, deck joists, rails, angles, couplings, pipings, etc., and all detail parts in engineering structures and machinery. This standardization, if accepted throughout the British Dominions, would permit of such a uniformity that a lost part, for example, in a reaping machine-bolts, nuts, plates, etc.-could be replaced by purchase from some local manufacturer, and thus a very large amount of time would be saved and a great convenience afforded to the users of such machinery. The parts of

a Canadian reaper sold in South Africa or New Zealand, for instance, could thus be forwarded from an adjacent hardware store. The aim of the Canadian Engineering Standards Association would be to provide for this standardization for Canada and to promote it by co-operation with the American standardization organizations. If it succeeds in bringing about standardization in Canada it will repay vastly more than the outlay that is likely to be involved. At present no work has been done in Canada on standardization of mechanical apparatus or parts. The field is an untouched one and it may be, therefore, a crusade of considerable magnitude to bring about the result desired. This association is comprised largely of trade engineers and it has to secure from the public a further $10,000. Their total expenditure this year they anticipate to he $20,000. They are not paid anything themselves, the work being purely voluntary. It was deemed a very good expenditure on the part of the Government to assist this voluntary organization by giving them a grant this year.
Is it a branch of the Manufacturers' Association?

No, it is not. The British Government renders the same assistance in Great Britain, as does the government in the United States. If we can have standardization in our products, it is generally conceded, there will be a great saving the world over and in our own country.
